definition: Panacea means a remedy for all ills or difficulties.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word panacea. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know panacea should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Every decade crowns a new kitchen panacea — vinegar, then kale, now fermented everything — and every decade the ailments outlast the trend.
A quick fix claims the least of all — it patches one symptom for today and may not hold till morning, while a panacea promises to heal every ill at once.
A remedy honestly treats one particular problem, but it stops short of a panacea, which claims to cure them all.

A cure-all is the plain, homely English word for a remedy claimed to mend every ill — the same sweeping promise a panacea makes. The difference is register: cure-all belongs on a medicine-show poster, while panacea is the formal, usually skeptical word writers reach for to puncture that claim.

An elixir is a magic potion promising health or long life — a wonder you could pour into a glass. A panacea makes a broader claim in any form: one remedy, policy, or plan said to cure every ill. Elixirs promise magic in a bottle; a panacea promises to mend all ills at once.

A magic bullet is one precise, almost effortless solution aimed at a single stubborn problem — one shot, one cure. A panacea claims far more territory: a single remedy for every ill at once. A magic bullet targets one disease; a panacea supposedly heals the whole ward.
the opposite promise — a dose that harms whatever it touches
the ruin or curse of a place, where a panacea would be its rescue

The Greeks made this word a goddess: Panakeia, 'all-healing,' daughter of the healer Asklepios. Her akos ('cure') built no other common English word, so panacea carries it alone. Fittingly, English has used the word with a raised eyebrow from the start — a cure claimed for everything usually cures nothing.
Panacea means a remedy for all ills or difficulties.
When the star quarterback transferred in, half the town saw him as a panacea for the losing streak.
The coach kept repeating that one arm could not block, kick, or cover; the line still leaked, the return game still fumbled, and the season ended 5 and 5 — better, but no miracle.
Panacea is the precise word because the town expected one remedy to fix every ill at once.
Solution would be too narrow — the passing game did get solved — and savior is melodrama; panacea names the specific fantasy of a single fix for all of it.
Panacea almost always appears with a wink or a warning — 'is no panacea' is its most common company, because the word names a claim too good to be true.
Use it to puncture oversold fixes; for something that honestly targets one problem, remedy or treatment is the straight word.

When the drought-hardy grain first reached the valley, the agency's brochures could not praise it enough.
It would end hunger, restore the soil, raise incomes, and keep the young from leaving for the city -- a panacea in a seed packet.
Farmers planted it, and it did grow where little else would.
But prices fell as harvests rose, the soil still needed rest, and the buses to the city stayed full.
The agronomist who had first imported the seed put it plainly: it was a good crop, and no crop can be a remedy for everything.
